newsitem.title: FRANCE: French divided over Chirac's justice reform plan.
newsitem.headline: French divided over Chirac's justice reform plan.

text.p: French politicians were divided on Tuesday over President Jacques Chirac's call for a far-reaching shake-up of the justice system, with some questioning the wisdom of making prosecutors independent of the political authorities.
In a broadcast to the nation on Monday night, Chirac called for greater independence for the judiciary, better protection of the presumption of innocence and simpler legal procedures.

Pierre Mazeaud, a senior jurist in Chirac's Gaullist RPR party who is chairman of parliament's legal committee, said he was reassured that the president had not set in concrete the aim of breaking the link between the public prosecutor and the political authorities.
It would be up to a bipartisan commission to think through the consequences of such a move, which Mazeaud has warned in the past could lead to "government by judges".

The Socialist opposition had mixed reactions. Former culture minister Jack Lang, himself a law professor, said no one should complain if Chirac at last launched a reform which the Socialists had long advocated.

"The president seems to be turning his back on his own (Gaullist) party's long tradition of tying up and domesticating the justice system," Lang told France Inter radio. "Let's take him at his word and look to the future."

But fellow Socialist Michel Sapin, a former junior justice minister, said Chirac's sudden interest in justice reform was suspicious at a time when magistrates were investigating alleged kickbacks to his Gaullist RPR party while he was mayor of Paris from 1977 to 1995.
"Difficult, complicated scandals with a potentially devastating political impact are ripening. So they are trying to create a windbreak," Sapin said.

Senator Michel Charasse, a former senior aide to the late president Francois Mitterrand, said the former Socialist head of state had always opposed making the public prosecutor's office independent of the government.

He quoted Mitterrand as having told his last cabinet meeting in 1995: "As an old man I speak to you with long experience of public life. I have been justice minister, a cabinet minister and president. I say to you: 'Never make the prosecutor's office independent. It would menace the republic."
